newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelans snap up CANTV shrs, issue starts strong.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelans snap up CANTV shrs, issue starts strong.

text.p: Now each time Venezuelan truck driver Antonio Mantilla uses his telephone he feels he will be earning rather than spending.
Mantilla is one of fifty thousand small Venezuelan investors seeking to buy a stake in national telephone company CANTV.
"It's the only real telephone company in the country, it's well run, and it has a great future," he said as he waited in a long queue outside a Caracas bank to place his order for shares.

Small Venezuelan investors had until Friday to buy shares under a preferential scheme that earmarked 50 million shares for the local market in the global 239 million share offering -- one of the largest to come out of Latin America this year.
Institutional Venezuelan investors can place orders Monday and Tuesday next week.
The reference price ranged from US$3.07 to $3.50, although the final price could be higher when it is finally settled on November 21.
"We're very pleased at how people have responded," said Agustin Cangas, president of Merinvest, one of the local lead syndicates.
Cangas said demand had crescendoed through the week after a slow start.
"Venezuelans always come through at the last moment, in the last hour, on the last day," he said.

But despite the hurry, Venezuelans have managed to place orders for some $105 million worth of shares, according to official figures, with demand particularly strong in the capital which enjoys a stronger financial culture.
According to government officials, orders placed for shares as of Thursday had topped $890 million. The government expects the issue to raise over $1 billion.
"The prospectuses arrived late ... so did the share order forms, but nevertheless it all went well," said one broker.

"In other countries, a privatisation such as this would have had six months' preparation. But here they had to change legislation, get congressional authorisation, and that all took up a lot of time," said Multinvest broker Jose Gregorio Tineo.
The share placement, seen by analysts as a litmus test of Venezuelan commitment to tough economic reforms is expected to send the Caracas bolsa for a loop.

Traders see CANTV shares, which will trade on Reuters screens as TDVd.CR, displacing current market leader Electricidad de Caracas from its top slot, and boosting market capitalisation from present levels of 3.6 trillion bolivars ($7.73 billion), according to stock exchange figures.
"It will completely change the bolsa and the attitude of Venezuelans towards savings and risk," said exchange President Alejandro Salcedo.
Active sessions on the bolsa are expected after CANTV shares begin to trade at the end of November.
"The whole market is going to rise," said Salcedo, adding the issue would also ready the bolsa for other large, expected initial public offerings.

State-owned holding company Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana is due to privatise its steel and aluminium producing arms early next year, with some ten percent of shares reserved for the Caracas bolsa.
Some see the boom more than doubling the bolsa's .IBC index by the end of 1997 to around 14,000.00 points.
"We expect a confluence of positive factors to double the value of (Caracas) shares over the next 12 months," investment bank Bear Stearns said in a recent research note.
On Friday, the index closed at 5,966.75.
-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600
